young elephant (bikka).  
Military training is of seven kinds: Drill (upasthána), turning 
(samvartana), advancing (samyána), trampling down and killing

assailing forts and cities (nágaráyanam), and warfare.

for the above training.

means to keep them under control is punishment. It has a 
suspicious aversion to work, is obstinate, of perverse nature, 
unsteady, willful, or of infatuated temper under the influence of 
rut.

purely roguish (suddha), clever in roguery (suvrata), perverse

under control shall be ascertained from the doctor of elephants.  
Tetherposts (álána), collars, girths, bridles, legchains, frontal

A hook, a bamboo staff, and machines (yantra) are

Necklaces such as vaijavantí and kshurapramála, and litter

answer:
As I taught in the Arthashastra, Book VIII, Chapter IV, my teacher held that pestilence is worse because it halts all work through disease, death, and the flight of servants, while famine stops no work and can even be productive of gold, cattle, and taxes. But I, Kautilya, dissent from this view.

I say famine is far graver. Pestilence devastates only a part of the country and can be remedied. Famine, however, causes trouble to the whole country and brings about a dearth of livelihood to all creatures. A partial affliction you can contain and recover from; a universal one leaves no foundation on which to rebuild.

For the modern leader, the parallel is clear: a crisis that cripples one department or one market (the pestilence) can be isolated and treated. A crisis that starves the entire organization of its lifeblood—cash flow, talent, supply—is an existential threat. Do not mistake the silent, creeping calamity for a lesser one because it lacks the immediate drama of disease.

I will answer directly, but I must first be plain with you: the retrieved passages do not contain a full doctrinal explanation from the Arthashastra of *why* a gift is powerful to influence someone. They state the claim and its practical application, not the underlying mechanism at length. So I will give you what is grounded here, and nothing invented beyond it.

The passage records that the Arthashastra "says that a gift is the most powerful medium that can influence anyone" (as cited in the commentary on 7.16.19). The verse itself teaches: "He should gratify, according to his power to help, one who has helped him" (Arthashastra 7.16.19).

From these two statements, the reasoning I can draw is this:

First, a gift, when given rightly, is a means of *gratification*. It does not merely transfer an object; it acknowledges a debt and binds the giver and receiver in goodwill. The verse does not say to bribe or buy loyalty. It says to *gratify* — to satisfy one who has helped you. That is a different mechanism from transaction. A bribe purchases a service; a gift, given according to one's power, purchases nothing. It builds obligation through gratitude, which is stronger than contract because it is voluntary on both sides.

Second, the same verse sets the limit: "according to his power to help." This means the gift's influence lies not in its price, but in its proportion. A king does not influence a minister by outspending the treasury beyond capacity; he influences by measuring the gift to the relationship. The passage says plainly: do not waste time thinking about whether to give, but "do not go out of the way to buy an expensive gift... buy the gift according to your capacity." The power of the gift is in the *fit* — timely, measured, and matched to the giver's means — not in extravagance, which corrupts the gesture into display or dependency.

So my answer from what is retrieved: a gift is powerful because it gratifies rather than transacts, and because it is governed by the giver's capacity, making it a gesture of judgment and goodwill, not merely of wealth. That is why it can influence where commands and payments cannot.

Chanakya was born with a full set of teeth. According to the monks, this was a sign that he would become a king in the future. While waiting for the emperor at the imperial court, Chanakya sat on the emperor's throne. A dasi (slave woman) courteously offered Chanakya the next seat, but Chanakya kept his kamandal (water pot) on it, while remaining seated on the throne. The servant offered him a choice of four more seats, but each time, he kept his various items on the seats, refusing to budge from the throne. Finally, the annoyed servant kicked him off the throne.
